On the following day both sides took all their cavalry—and Publius also the javelin-throwers from among his infantry—and advanced across the plain, eager to scout out each other's forces.

As soon as they drew near and saw the dust rising up, they at once began to form up for battle.

Publius, placing his javelin-throwers and the Gallic cavalry that accompanied them in front, and stationing the rest in a line abreast, advanced at a walking pace.

Hannibal, drawing up his bridled cavalry and all the steadier part of his horse facing the front, went to meet the enemy, while he held the Numidian cavalry ready on each wing for an encircling movement.

Since both the commanders and the horsemen on each side were keen for the contest, the first clash turned out to be such that the javelin-throwers did not even manage to let fly their first missile, but reeled back and fled at once through the gaps to the rear of their own squadrons, panicked by the charge and terrified of being trampled by the cavalry bearing down on them.

Those who met one another face to face kept the contest evenly balanced for a long time;

for it was at once a cavalry battle and an infantry battle, because of the number of men who dismounted in the very midst of the fighting.

But when the Numidians had encircled them and fallen on them from behind, the foot javelin-throwers, who at first had escaped the cavalry clash, were now trampled down by the mass and the onslaught of the Numidians;

while those who from the start had been fighting the Carthaginians face to face—having lost many of their own men, but having destroyed still more of the Carthaginians—now, attacked from the rear by the Numidians, were put to flight: most of them scattered, but some rallied around their commander.

## Book 3 Chapter 66: Scipio Crosses the Po

Publius then broke camp and advanced across the plains toward the bridge over the Padus, in haste to get his legions across first.

For seeing that the ground was level, that the enemy was superior in cavalry, and that he himself was weighed down by his wound, he judged it necessary to bring his forces back to safety.

Hannibal for a while supposed that they would risk a battle with their infantry too; but when he saw that they had moved out of their camp, he followed as far as the first river and the bridge over it.

Finding that most of the planks had been torn up, but that the men guarding the bridge were still left behind near the river, he took these prisoner—about six hundred of them in number.

Then, hearing that the rest had already gotten a long way ahead, he turned about again in the opposite direction and made his march along the river, hurrying to reach a point on the Padus where it could easily be bridged.

On the second day he halted and bridged the crossing with river boats, and assigned to Hasdrubal the task of bringing the main body across, while he himself crossed at once and dealt with the envoys who had arrived from the neighboring districts.

For as soon as he had gained the advantage, all the neighboring Celts hastened, in keeping with their original intention, to become his friends, to supply him, and to join the Carthaginians on campaign.

After receiving those who had come in a friendly manner and bringing his forces over from the far side, he advanced along the river, taking the opposite direction to his earlier march: for he now made his way downstream, eager to come to grips with the enemy.

Publius, having crossed the Padus and encamped near the city of Placentia, which was a Roman colony, attended at once to himself and the other wounded, and at the same time, considering that he had brought his forces into a safe position, kept quiet.

Hannibal, arriving on the second day after his crossing near the enemy, on the third day drew up his army in full view of his opponents.

But when no one came out against him, he pitched camp, leaving an interval of about fifty stades between the two armies.

## Book 3 Chapter 67: The Gauls Join Hannibal

The Celts who were serving alongside the Romans, seeing that the Carthaginians' prospects were the more promising of the two, made an agreement among themselves and watched for the right moment to strike, each remaining meanwhile in his own tent.

After the men in the camp had eaten their supper and gone to sleep, the Celts let most of the night pass, and then, around the time of the morning watch, they armed themselves and fell upon the Romans encamped nearest to them.

They killed many of them and wounded a good number more; and in the end, after cutting off the heads of the dead, they withdrew to the Carthaginians, numbering about two thousand infantry and a little under two hundred cavalry.

Hannibal welcomed their arrival warmly. He at once encouraged them, promised each of them suitable rewards, and sent them off to their own cities to report to their fellow citizens what they had done and to urge them to join his alliance.

For he knew that, once they learned of the act of treachery committed against the Romans by their own countrymen, they would all be compelled to throw in their lot with him.

At the same time the Boii also arrived and handed over to him the three men whom the Romans had sent out to distribute the land—men whom they had seized at the very start of the war by breaking the truce, as I have already described above.

Hannibal welcomed their goodwill and gave pledges of friendship and alliance to those who had come; but he returned the men to them, instructing them to keep them safe, so that through them they might recover their own hostages, in keeping with their original purpose.

Publius, indignant at the treachery that had occurred, reasoned that since the Celts had long been hostile toward the Romans, the defection of these men would cause all the surrounding Gauls to go over to the Carthaginians; and so he decided that he must guard against what was coming.

For this reason, when night fell, he broke camp toward dawn and set out toward the river Trebia and the hills adjoining it, trusting in the strength of the terrain

## Book 3 Chapter 68: Tiberius Sempronius Joins Scipio

and in the support of the allies who lived nearby. When Hannibal learned that they had broken camp, he immediately sent out the Numidian cavalry, and shortly afterward the rest, while he himself followed close behind with his main army.

The Numidians, finding the camp deserted, set it on fire.

This proved a great benefit to the Romans; for if the Numidians had instead pressed on at their heels and overtaken the baggage train, many of the Romans would have been cut down by the cavalry on the open plains.

As it was, however, most of them managed to cross the river Trebia first; of those left behind in the rearguard, some were killed and others taken alive by the Carthaginians.

Publius, then, having crossed the river just mentioned, made camp on the first line of hills,

and after surrounding his position with a ditch and a palisade, he waited for Tiberius and the forces with him, while attending carefully to his own recovery, eager to be able to take part in the coming engagement.

Hannibal pitched his camp about forty stades away from the enemy.

The mass of the Celts who inhabited the plains, having committed themselves to the Carthaginians' hopes, supplied the army abundantly with provisions and were ready to share in every undertaking and danger alongside Hannibal.

The people in Rome, when news of the cavalry engagement reached them, were taken aback that the outcome had run contrary to their expectations; yet they were not at a loss for excuses to convince themselves that what had happened was not a defeat.

Some blamed the rashness of the general, others the deliberate treachery of the Celts, which they inferred from the latter's recent defection.

In general, since their infantry legions remained intact, they reckoned their hopes for the overall outcome were likewise intact.

And so, when Tiberius and the legions with him arrived and were marching through Rome, the people imagined that the mere sight of them would decide the battle.

When the soldiers had gathered at Ariminum in accordance with their oath, the general took them up and led them forward, hurrying to join Publius's forces.

Having effected the junction and pitched camp beside them with his own troops, he let his men recover their strength—for they had marched on foot continuously for forty days from Lilybaeum to Ariminum—while he made every preparation as if for battle,

and he himself conferred carefully with Publius, inquiring into what had already taken place and deliberating together about the present situation.

## Book 3 Chapter 69: A Skirmish Near the Trebia

Around this same time Hannibal, by an act of treachery, gained control of the town of Clastidium, which was surrendered to him by the man from Brundisium to whom the Romans had entrusted it.

Having become master of the garrison and the stores of grain, he used the grain for his immediate needs, but took the men he had captured along with him unharmed,

wishing to give a demonstration of his own policy, so that those caught up by the circumstances need not be afraid or despair of obtaining safety from him.

He honored the traitor lavishly, eager to entice those holding positions of authority over toward the Carthaginians' prospects.

After this, observing that certain Celts who lived between the Padus and the river Trebia had made a friendship with him while at the same time sending messages to the Romans—convinced that in this way they would secure their safety from both sides—

he sent out two thousand infantry and about a thousand cavalry, both Celts and Numidians, with orders to overrun their territory.

When these men had carried out their orders and gathered a great deal of plunder, the Celts immediately came to the Roman camp begging for help.

Tiberius, who had long been looking for an opportunity to act, now seized on this as a pretext and sent out the greater part of his cavalry, together with about a thousand javelin-throwers from his infantry.

When these troops quickly came up with the enemy across the Trebia and fought them for the plunder, the Celts and Numidians were put to flight and withdrew toward their own camp.

But the troops on guard in front of the Carthaginian camp quickly grasped what was happening and brought up reserves from there to help the hard-pressed men; whereupon the Romans in turn were routed and withdrew back to their own camp.

Tiberius, seeing what was happening, sent out all his cavalry and javelin-throwers. When this happened, the Celts again gave way and retreated to the safety of their own position.

The Carthaginian general, being unprepared to risk a decisive engagement and believing that one should never bring on a full-scale battle without a settled plan or on the strength of any chance opening—which, it must be said, is the mark of a good commander—

checked his own men as they drew near the camp and forced them to halt and turn about, but prevented them from pursuing and engaging the enemy, recalling them through his aides and trumpeters. The Romans, after waiting a short time, withdrew,

having lost only a few of their own men while destroying a greater number of the Carthaginians.

## Book 3 Chapter 70: Tiberius Sempronius Plans to Attack

Tiberius, elated and overjoyed at this success, was keen to decide the whole issue as quickly as possible.

Now it lay within his power to act on his own judgment in the present circumstances, since Publius was ill; nevertheless, wishing to secure his colleague's opinion as well, he discussed the matter with him.

Publius, however, held the opposite view about the present situation.

For he reckoned that their legions would become better after wintering under arms; that the faithlessness of the Celts would not remain loyal once the Carthaginians were inactive and forced to keep quiet, but would instead make some fresh move against them again;

and besides, that once he himself had recovered from his wound, he hoped to be able to render real service to their common cause.

Reasoning along these lines, he urged Tiberius to remain with things as they stood.

Tiberius knew that each of these points was being stated truly and properly; but driven by ambition and an unreasonable confidence in the situation, he was eager to decide the whole matter himself—before Publius could be present at the battle and before the incoming consuls could take over the command; for the time for that was now at hand.

For this reason, choosing not the moment that the circumstances called for but his own, he was plainly bound to fall short of what was needed.

Hannibal, holding much the same view as Publius about the present situation, was for the opposite reason eager to engage the enemy: first, he wished to make use of the Celts' fighting spirit while it was still fresh;

second, to engage the Roman legions while they were still untrained and newly recruited; third, to fight while Publius was still unable to take the field; and, most important of all, to be doing something and not let the time slip away to no purpose.

For when a general has brought his army into foreign territory and is attempting bold undertakings, this is the one means of safety: continually to keep the hopes of his allies fresh.

Hannibal, then, knowing the attack that was to come

## Book 3 Chapter 71: Hannibal Prepares An Ambush

These were the matters that occupied Tiberius. Hannibal, meanwhile, had long since noticed a stretch of ground between the two camps that was flat and bare of trees, yet well suited for an ambush, because a watercourse ran through it with a raised bank along its edge, and along that bank grew a continuous thicket of thorns and brambles. There he set about laying a trap for the enemy.

He was confident the scheme would easily escape notice. For the Romans were suspicious of wooded ground, since the Celts always set their ambushes in such places, but they felt no distrust of level and open country—

not realizing that, both for staying concealed and for keeping the men in ambush from coming to any harm, open ground is in fact better suited than woodland. The reason is that those lying in wait can see everything that is going on from a long way off, while in most such places there is cover enough to hide behind.

A chance watercourse with a low bank, or sometimes reeds, ferns, and a kind of thorn-scrub, can conceal not only infantry but at times even cavalry, provided one takes the modest precaution of laying the conspicuous parts of the armor flat against the ground and tucking the helmets in under the shields.

In any case, the Carthaginian general, after conferring with his brother Mago and with his council about the coming engagement, found them all in agreement with his plans.

So, as soon as the army had taken its evening meal, he called for his brother Mago—a young man, but full of dash and trained in warfare from boyhood—and assigned to him a hundred horsemen and an equal number of foot soldiers.

While it was still daylight, he had picked out the most robust men from the whole army and ordered them, after their supper, to report to his tent.

There he encouraged them and roused in them the spirit the occasion demanded, and instructed each man to choose ten of the bravest soldiers from his own unit and bring them to a certain spot in the camp that had already been designated.

When they had carried out his orders, he sent these men—a thousand cavalry and as many infantry—off by night to the place of ambush, supplying them with guides, and gave his brother his instructions about the timing of the attack.

At first light he himself assembled the Numidian cavalry, who were outstanding for their stamina, encouraged them, and—promising rewards to those who fought well—ordered them to ride up to the enemy's rampart, then quickly cross the river and skirmish so as to provoke the enemy into action. His aim was to catch his opponents before they had breakfasted and while they were still unprepared for what lay ahead.

He then gathered the rest of his officers, urged them likewise toward the coming battle, and ordered them all to breakfast and to see to their weapons and horses.

## Book 3 Chapter 72: Preparations for Battle

As soon as Tiberius saw the Numidian cavalry approaching, he immediately sent out his own cavalry on their own, with orders to engage and close with the enemy.

Next he sent out the foot javelineers, about six thousand of them, and he also set the rest of his army in motion from the camp, as though the whole issue were going to be decided at first sight. He was emboldened both by his superior numbers and by his cavalry's success the day before.

It was now around the winter solstice, and the day was snowy and bitterly cold; and since nearly all the men and horses had marched out without breakfast, at the start the troops were carried along by their dash and eagerness.

But when it came to crossing the river Trebia, which had risen because of the rain that had fallen during the night on the high ground above the camps, the infantry could barely get across, immersed up to their chests.

As a result the army was in distress from the cold and from hunger, all the more as the day wore on.

The Carthaginians, by contrast, had eaten and drunk in their tents, had got their horses ready, and were all rubbing themselves down with oil and arming around their fires.

Hannibal, watching for his moment, as soon as he saw that the Romans had crossed the river, threw out his spearmen and Balearic slingers—some eight thousand of them—as a covering force and led out his army.

Advancing about eight stades in front of his camp, he drew up his infantry, about twenty thousand in number—Iberians, Celts, and Libyans—in a single straight line,

and dividing his cavalry, he stationed them on either wing—more than ten thousand, counting his Celtic allies—while he split the elephants and posted them in front of both wings.

Tiberius at this same moment was recalling his cavalry, since he saw they could make no headway against the enemy. For the Numidians would fall back easily and in scattered fashion, then wheel about and press the attack again boldly and recklessly—this being the characteristic feature of Numidian fighting.

His infantry he drew up in the formation customary among the Romans: about sixteen thousand citizens and twenty thousand allies.

For with them a full army for major operations consists of that many men, whenever circumstances bring both consuls together at once.

After this, placing his cavalry—about four thousand—on either wing, he advanced against the enemy in imposing style, in good order

## Book 3 Chapter 73: The Battle of the Trebia

and at a steady, deliberate pace. When the two sides were now close to one another, the light-armed troops posted in front of each army closed with each other.

When this happened, the Romans were at a disadvantage in many respects, while for the Carthaginians the engagement turned out greatly in their favor,

since the Roman foot javelineers had been under hard strain since dawn, had spent most of their missiles in the clash with the Numidians, and found the missiles they had left useless from being soaked through by the persistent damp.

Much the same was happening with their cavalry and with the army as a whole.

With the Carthaginians the situation was the very opposite: drawn up fresh and in their prime, they were always ready and eager for whatever was needed.

And so, as soon as the light troops who had fought the opening skirmish had been received back through the gaps in the line, and the heavy-armed troops on both sides had clashed, the Carthaginian cavalry at once began pressing the enemy hard from both wings, since they far outnumbered them and were superior in the freshness of both men and horses, owing to the unworn condition I mentioned, in which they had set out.

As the Roman cavalry gave way and the wings of the phalanx were left exposed, the Carthaginian spearmen and the mass of Numidians, sweeping past their own front ranks and falling upon the Roman flanks, did them great damage and prevented them from fighting the troops facing them.

But the heavy-armed troops on both sides, who held the front and center positions of the whole line, kept up a close, hand-to-hand fight for a long time, evenly matched,

## Book 3 Chapter 74: The Romans Retreat to Placentia

making the contest a fierce one. It was at this point that the Numidians lying in ambush rose up and suddenly fell on the rear of the troops fighting in the center, throwing the Roman forces into great confusion and difficulty.

In the end both of Tiberius's wings, pressed in front by the elephants and all around—on their flanks—by the light-armed troops, were routed and driven, as the pursuit went on, toward the river that lay behind them.

After this, of the Romans stationed in the center of the action, those positioned in the rear were destroyed and suffered terribly under the attack of the men from the ambush,

while those in the foremost ranks, forced to fight on, overpowered the Celts and a portion of the Libyans, killed many of them, and cut their way through the Carthaginian line.

Seeing that their own wings had been driven off the field, they gave up any thought of going to their aid or of returning to their own camp—wary of the enemy's superior numbers of cavalry, and hindered by the river and by the driving, swirling downpour beating down on their heads.

So, keeping their ranks, they withdrew in a body and in safety to Placentia, numbering no fewer than ten thousand.

Of the rest, the greater part perished near the river at the hands of the elephants and the cavalry,

while those of the infantry who escaped, and most of the cavalry, made their withdrawal toward the body of men just mentioned and were brought back together with them to Placentia.

The Carthaginian army pursued the enemy as far as the river but, unable to advance any farther because of the storm, returned again to its camp.

They were all overjoyed at the battle, feeling they had won a complete success; for it turned out that few of the Iberians and Libyans had fallen, and that the heaviest losses had been among the Celts.

But from the rain and the snow that followed, they were so badly affected that the elephants died—all but one—and many of the men and horses perished as well from the cold.

## Book 3 Chapter 75: Better Success in Spain

Tiberius, well aware of what had happened but wishing as far as possible to hide the disaster from the people in Rome, sent messengers to report that a battle had been fought but that the storm had robbed them of the victory.

For the moment the Romans believed the reports that reached them; but before long they learned that the Carthaginians were holding their own camp and that all the Celts had gone over to friendship with them,

while their own men had abandoned their camp, had withdrawn from the field, had all gathered together into the cities, and were being supplied with necessities by sea up the river Padus. They then understood all too clearly what had really happened in the battle.

And so, since the affair had come upon them as a complete surprise, they devoted themselves with special energy to their remaining preparations and to guarding the regions that lay exposed, sending legions to Sardinia and Sicily, and garrisons to Tarentum and to other places of strategic value; they also fitted out sixty quinqueremes.

Gnaeus Servilius and Gaius Flaminius, who happened to be the consuls newly installed at that time, were assembling the allies and enrolling their own legions.

They also forwarded supplies, some to Ariminum and some to Etruria, with the intention of taking the field from those positions.

They sent too to Hiero asking for help, and he dispatched to them five hundred Cretans and a thousand peltasts. In short, they were vigorously making every kind of preparation on every front.

For the Romans are at their most formidable, both collectively and as individuals, when they are gripped by genuine fear.

## Book 3 Chapter 76: Gnaeus Scipio in Spain

About this same time Gnaeus Cornelius, who had been left by his brother Publius in command of the naval forces (as I mentioned earlier), set sail from the mouths of the Rhone and put in with his whole fleet on the Iberian coast at the region called Emporium.

Starting from there he made a series of landings: those of the coastal inhabitants who would not submit, as far as the river Iber, he besieged, while those who came over to him he treated kindly, taking every possible care for their welfare.

Having secured the coastal peoples who had joined him, he advanced with his whole army, marching into the interior,

for by now he had also gathered a large allied contingent of Iberians. As he went forward he won some cities over and subdued others.

When the Carthaginians—those whom Hanno had been left in charge of in that district—encamped against him near a city called Cissa, Gnaeus engaged them in a pitched battle, defeated them, and gained a great quantity of property, since the whole baggage of the forces that had set out for Italy had been left behind with them.

He made allies and friends of all the peoples north of the river Iber, and took prisoner both Hanno, the Carthaginian general, and Andobales, the leader of the Iberians.

This Andobales was ruler of the inland regions and had always been exceptionally well disposed toward the Carthaginians.

Hasdrubal quickly grasped what had happened and came to the rescue, crossing the river Iber.

Learning that the men from the Roman fleet had been left behind and were carrying on carelessly and overconfidently because of the success of the land forces,

he took from his own army about eight thousand infantry and around a thousand cavalry, caught the men from the ships scattered about the countryside, killed many of them, and forced the rest to flee to their vessels.

He then withdrew, recrossed the river Iber, and set about preparing and garrisoning the regions south of the river, taking up his winter quarters at New Carthage.

Gnaeus, having rejoined his fleet and punished those responsible for the disaster according to their own customs, then brought his land and sea forces together in one place and took up his winter quarters at Tarraco.

By dividing the spoils fairly among his soldiers, he won great goodwill from them and made them eager for what lay ahead.

## Book 3 Chapter 77: Hannibal's Treatment of Roman Prisoners

Such was the state of affairs in Iberia. As the spring season set in, Gaius Flaminius took up his forces and advanced through Etruria, pitching camp before the city of the Arretines,

while Gnaeus Servilius went in the opposite direction, toward Ariminum, to watch there for the enemy's invasion.

Hannibal, wintering in Celtic territory, kept the Romans among the prisoners from the battle under guard, giving them only modest rations,

but their allies he at first treated with every kindness; and afterward he gathered them together and addressed them, declaring that he had not come to make war on them but on the Romans on their behalf. Therefore, he said, if they were sensible, they should

hold fast to friendship with him.

For he had come, first, to win back freedom for the peoples of Italy, and likewise to help each of them recover the cities and territory they had lost to the Romans.

With these words he released them all without ransom to their own homes, wishing in this way both to draw the inhabitants of Italy to his side and to alienate them from their goodwill toward Rome, and to stir up those who felt they had suffered any loss of cities or harbors under Roman rule.

## Book 3 Chapter 78: Hannibal Marches Southward

During his time in winter quarters he also employed a certain stratagem that was thoroughly Phoenician in character.

Because he was anxious about the unreliability of the Celts and about possible plots against his life—the alliance between himself and them being so recently formed—he had a set of false hairpieces made, each one suited to the appearance natural to a different age of life.

These he wore constantly, changing them from one to another, and in the same way he kept changing his clothing as well, always to match whichever wig he was wearing.

By this means he was hard to recognize, not only for those who caught sight of him suddenly, but even for those who were on familiar terms with him.

He observed, however, that the Celts were resentful at the war dragging on in their own territory, and that they were eager and on edge to push into enemy land—ostensibly out of anger toward the Romans, but mostly for the sake of plunder. He therefore decided to break camp as quickly as possible and to satisfy the army's impulses.

And so, as soon as the season began to change, he made inquiries of those reputed to have the best knowledge of the country. He found that the other routes for invading enemy territory were long and obvious to the enemy, whereas the one leading through the marshes into Etruria, though difficult, was short and would catch Flaminius and his men completely off guard.

Since he was always by temperament drawn to this kind of approach, he resolved to make his march by this route.

But when word spread through the camp that the general intended to lead them through some marshes, every man grew wary of the march, fearful of pits and

## Book 3 Chapter 79: Hannibal Goes Through the Marsh

the swampy stretches of the terrain. But Hannibal had carefully reconnoitered the ground along the route, learning which parts were shallow and firm. He broke camp and placed the Libyans and Iberians—all the more serviceable part of his force—in the vanguard, mixing the baggage train in among them so that they would have ample supplies for the immediate present.

As for the longer term, he gave no thought at all to the whole baggage train, reasoning that once he reached enemy country, if he were defeated he would have no further need of supplies, and if he held the open field he would have no shortage of provisions.

Behind the troops just mentioned he set the Celts, and behind all of them the cavalry.

He left his brother Mago in charge of the rearguard, both for general reasons and especially because of the softness and aversion to hardship of the Celts, so that if they should suffer and try to turn back, Mago could stop them with the cavalry and lay hands on them.

Now the Iberians and Libyans, marching through the marshes while these were still untrampled, got through with only moderate hardship, since they were all hardy by nature and accustomed to such ordeals.

But the Celts advanced only with difficulty, since the marshes were now churned up and trodden into deep mire, and they endured the suffering painfully and miserably, being wholly unused to that kind of distress.

Yet they were prevented from slipping back to the rear by the cavalry stationed behind them.

All of them suffered, especially from sleeplessness, as they marched continuously through water for four days and three nights on end; but the Celts in particular labored and perished more than the rest.

Most of his pack animals slipped in the mud, fell, and died, providing a single service to the men in their fall:

for the soldiers sat on the carcasses and, piling the baggage in heaps, kept themselves above the water, and in this way snatched a little sleep during a short part of the night.

Not a few of the horses, too, lost their hoofs through the relentless march across the mud.

Hannibal himself barely came through, riding with great hardship on the one elephant that survived, in severe pain from a violent attack of ophthalmia that had struck him—through which he ultimately lost the sight of one eye, since the circumstances allowed him no time to halt or apply treatment, the situation making it impossible.

## Book 3 Chapter 80: Flaminius in Hannibal's Way

Having crossed the marshy terrain in this unexpected fashion, and finding Flaminius in Etruria encamped before the city of Arretium, Hannibal for the moment pitched camp there beside the marshes,

wishing to rest his army and to make a thorough study of the enemy and of the terrain that lay ahead.

He learned that the country in front of him was rich in plunder, and that Flaminius was a consummate rabble-rouser and demagogue but had no natural aptitude for the genuine conduct of military affairs, and on top of this was overconfident in his own resources.

He therefore calculated that if he marched past their camp and descended into the territory beyond, Flaminius—partly anxious about the jeers of the crowd, unable to bear watching the land being ravaged, and partly stung by personal feeling—would readily come along, following him into any region, eager to win the success on his own and not to wait for the arrival of his colleague, who held equal authority.

From all this he reckoned that Flaminius would hand him many openings for an attack.

## Book 3 Chapter 81: A General Must Know his Enemy's Character

He reasoned all this out with intelligence and practical sense. For it would not be wrong to say that anyone who supposes there is any more decisive element of generalship than knowing the purpose and character of the opposing commander is ignorant and deluded.

Just as in contests between individuals or between ranks the man who means to win must observe carefully how he can reach his goal and what part of his opponent appears exposed or insufficiently armored,

so too those in command of whole armies must look not for where some part of the body is unguarded, but for where some vulnerable point in the mind of the enemy commander shows itself.

For many men, through laziness and sheer idleness, utterly throw away not only the affairs of the state but their own private lives as well;

many, through their craving for wine, cannot even fall asleep without a stupefying bout of drunkenness;

and some, through their lust for sexual pleasure and their obsession with it, have not only brought ruin on cities and lives but have even forfeited their own existence in disgrace.

And indeed, cowardice and slackness bring reproach on the individuals who have them privately, but when they reside in a supreme commander they become a public matter and the greatest of calamities.

For such a commander not only renders his subordinates ineffective, but often brings the gravest dangers upon those who have placed their trust in him.

Recklessness, too, and audacity and irrational temper, and likewise vainglory and conceit, are easy prey for the enemy but most perilous for one's friends. For a man of that sort is an easy mark for every plot, ambush, and deception.

So if a man can discern the failings of those around him, and approach his adversaries precisely at the point and by the means through which the enemy's leader is most vulnerable, he would very quickly master the whole campaign. For just as, if you remove the helmsman from a ship,

the entire vessel with all its crew falls into the hands of the enemy, in the same way, if a man outmaneuvers the commander of an army through his designs and calculations, he often gains possession of the opposing force, men and all.

It was precisely by foreseeing and reasoning out these things about the enemy commander that Hannibal, on this occasion, did not fail in his design.

## Book 3 Chapter 82: Flaminius Enticed Out

For as soon as Hannibal broke camp from the region around Faesulae and, passing a little beyond the Roman encampment, made his raid into the country that lay ahead,

Flaminius at once became agitated and full of fury, imagining that he was being treated with contempt by the enemy.

Then, as the country was being plundered and the smoke rising everywhere signaled its devastation, he grew indignant, regarding what was happening as outrageous.

And so, when some advised that he should not rashly pursue or close with the enemy, but should be on his guard and beware of their large body of cavalry, and above all should wait for the other consul and engage in battle only when all the armies were combined together,

he not only paid no attention to what they said but could not even tolerate those who offered such advice.

He urged them rather to consider what the people back home were likely to say if the country were being ravaged almost up to the very walls of Rome while they sat encamped in Etruria behind the enemy.

Finally, with these words, he broke camp and advanced with his army, giving no thought to time or place, intent only on engaging the enemy, as though victory were already plainly theirs.

For he had instilled in the crowds such confident expectation that those who tagged along outside the ranks for the sake of booty—carrying chains and fetters and all such equipment—were more numerous than those bearing arms.

Hannibal, for his part, was at the same time advancing forward through Etruria toward Rome, keeping on his left the city called Cortona and its hills, and on his right the lake called Thrasymene.

As he advanced he set fire to the country and laid it waste, wishing to provoke the fury of his opponents. And when he saw that Flaminius was already drawing near,

and had observed ground naturally suited to his purpose,

## Book 3 Chapter 83: Hannibal Takes a Position in the Valley

he set about preparing for battle. Along the route there was a level defile, which on its two long sides had high, continuous hills, while at its short ends it was closed: on the side facing him by a steep, hard-to-climb height set across the way, and at the rear by the lake, which left only an extremely narrow passage into the valley along the foot of the hills.

Passing through the valley along the lake, Hannibal seized for himself the hill that faced the line of march, and encamped on it with the Iberians and Libyans.

The Balearic slingers and spearmen he led around by the vanguard and posted in concealment beneath the hills lying to the right of the valley, deploying them in a long extended line.

The cavalry and the Celts he likewise led around in a circuit under the hills on the left and stretched them out in a continuous line, so that the outermost of them were right at the entrance—the one running between the lake and the foot of the hills into the place described.

So Hannibal, having made these preparations during the night and having ringed the valley with his ambushes, kept quiet.

Flaminius followed close behind, eager to close with the enemy.

He had pitched camp the day before right beside the lake at a very late hour, and when day broke afterward he immediately, at dawn, led his vanguard along the lake into the valley below, intending to engage the enemy.

## Book 3 Chapter 84: The Disaster At the Thrasymene Lake

The day being exceptionally foggy, Hannibal—once the greater part of the marching column had entered the valley and the enemy's vanguard was already drawing close to him—gave the signals and sent word to the men in the ambushes, and launched his attack on the enemy from every side at once.

Flaminius and his men, taken aback by this sudden appearance, and with visibility poor because of the conditions in the air, and with the enemy bearing down and falling upon them from higher ground at many points, found that the Roman company-commanders and tribunes were not only unable to bring help wherever it was needed, but could not even grasp what was happening.

For they were being struck simultaneously—some in front, some from the rear, some on the flanks.

As a result, most of them were cut down still in their order of march, unable to defend themselves, as if they had been handed over to slaughter by the poor judgment of their commander.

For while they were still debating what to do, they were being destroyed before they realized it.

At that very moment some of the Celts fell upon Flaminius himself—who was at a loss and in utter distress over the whole situation—and killed him.

So of the Romans in the valley nearly fifteen thousand fell, unable either to give way to the circumstances or to do anything at all, but holding to this above all else, in keeping with their training: not to flee or abandon their ranks.

Those, however, who were caught on the march in the narrows between the lake and the foot of the hills were destroyed shamefully, and still more wretchedly.

For as they were forced back into the lake, some, in their frenzy of mind, plunged in to swim with their armor on and were drowned, while the great mass advanced into the lake as far as they could and stayed there with only their heads above the water.

When the cavalry rode in and destruction was plainly before them, they raised their hands and begged to be taken alive, uttering every kind of plea; but in the end they were killed, some by the enemy, and some at their own urging by their comrades.

About six thousand of those in the valley, having beaten the enemy directly in front of them, were unable to come to the aid of their own side or to get around behind their opponents, because they could see nothing of what was happening—though they could have rendered great service to the overall outcome.

Always pressing forward, they kept advancing, convinced they would fall in with some of the enemy, until without realizing it they emerged onto the higher ground. When they reached the heights,

and the fog had by now lifted, they understood the disaster that had occurred. No longer able to do anything—since the enemy now had the upper hand in the whole battle and already held all the ground—they closed ranks and withdrew to a certain Etrurian village.

After the battle, Maharbal was sent by the general with the Iberians and the spearmen and encamped around the village; and with manifold difficulties closing in on them, they laid down their arms and surrendered under a truce, on the understanding that their lives would be spared.

Such, then, was the course of the entire engagement that took place in Etruria between the Romans and the Carthaginians.

## Book 3 Chapter 85: Roman Reaction

So that affair was brought to its conclusion. Hannibal, once the men who had surrendered under terms had been brought back to him, along with the rest of the prisoners as well, gathered them all together — more than fifteen thousand of them.

He began by making clear that Maharbal had no authority to grant the men who had surrendered their safety without his own consent. After this he delivered an indictment against the Romans.

When he had finished with that, he distributed all the captives who were Romans among the units of his army to be held under guard, but he released all the allies, without ransom, to return to their own homes,

repeating the same declaration he had made before: that he had come to wage war not against the Italians but against the Romans, on behalf of the freedom of the Italians.

He then let his own forces recover their strength, and he buried the most distinguished of the dead from his own army, about thirty in number; for in all about fifteen hundred had fallen, most of whom were Celts.

Having done this, he began to deliberate with his brother and his friends about where and how he ought to press his advance, since he was now confident about the whole campaign.

When news of the disaster that had occurred reached Rome, the leaders of the state were unable to disguise or play down what had happened, because of the sheer scale of the calamity, and they were forced to tell the people what had taken place, calling the citizens together into an assembly.

And so, the moment the magistrate announced to the crowds from the Rostra, "We have lost a great battle," such a panic broke out that, to those who had been present on both occasions, the event then seemed far greater than at the actual moment of the battle itself.

And this was natural enough. For having had no experience, for many years, either of the word or of the fact of an acknowledged defeat, they bore the reversal with no moderation and no composure.

The Senate, however, did not do so: it held to the reasoning that the situation demanded, and deliberated about the future — how, and what, each group ought to do.

## Book 3 Chapter 86: A Second Disaster in Etruria

At the time of the battle, Gnaeus Servilius, the consul stationed forward in the region of Ariminum —

this lies on the side of Italy facing the Adriatic, where the plains of Gaul join the rest of Italy, not far from where the mouths of the Po empty into the sea —

having heard that Hannibal had invaded Etruria and was encamped opposite Flaminius, intended to join all his own legions to him. But, unable to do so because of the weight of his army, he hurriedly sent Gaius Centenius ahead with four thousand cavalry, wishing them to arrive in advance of his own coming, should circumstances require it.

Hannibal, when the enemy's relief force was reported to him after the battle, sent out Maharbal with the spearmen and a portion of the cavalry.

These troops fell upon Gaius's men and, in the very first engagement, destroyed nearly half of them, and after driving the rest together onto a certain hill, on the following day took them all prisoner.

In Rome, with the report of the battle now three days old, and the suffering throughout the city at that very moment, so to speak, at its most inflamed, when this further reversal also came on top of it, not only the populace but the Senate itself was thrown into dismay.

For this reason they set aside the annual conduct of public business and the election of magistrates, and undertook to deliberate more seriously about the present situation, judging that affairs and the surrounding circumstances called for a commander with absolute authority.

Hannibal, now thoroughly confident about the whole campaign, decided against approaching Rome for the present, and instead advanced through the countryside, plundering it without resistance, making his march toward the Adriatic.

Passing through the country called Umbria and that of Picenum, he reached the Adriatic region on the tenth day,

having taken so much plunder that the army could neither drive nor carry off the spoils, and having killed a great many people along the way;

for, just as in the storming of cities, on this occasion too an order had been given to kill any grown men who fell into their hands. This he did because of the

## Book 3 Chapter 87: Quintus Fabius Maximus

innate hatred toward the Romans that was rooted in him. During this period, encamping beside the Adriatic in a country surpassingly rich in every kind of produce, he took great pains over the recovery and care of his men, and no less of his horses.

For since their winter quarters in the region of Gaul had been spent in the open, and what with the cold and the lack of oil for grooming, and on top of that the subsequent march and hardship through the marshes, nearly all the horses, and likewise the men, had developed what is called scurvy and a wretched condition of that sort.

So, having gained control of a prosperous country, he put the horses back into good condition, and restored the bodies and the spirits of his soldiers. He also re-equipped the Libyans in the Roman fashion with select weapons, since he had become master of so much captured gear.

At this time he also sent men by sea to report to Carthage about what had happened; for this was the first time he had reached the sea since he made his invasion into Italy.

On hearing this, the Carthaginians rejoiced greatly, and gave much energy and forethought to supporting in every possible way both their cause in Italy and their cause in Iberia.

The Romans appointed as dictator Quintus Fabius, a man outstanding in judgment and of fine natural endowment. Indeed, even down to our own day the members of this household are called the Maximi — that is, "the Greatest" — on account of that man's successes and achievements.

The dictator differs from the consuls in this respect: each of the consuls is attended by twelve axes,

but this officer by twenty-four; and whereas the consuls in many matters require the Senate's cooperation to carry out their plans, this man is a commander with absolute power, upon whose appointment all the magistracies in Rome are immediately dissolved, except the tribunes of the people.

We shall, however, give a more precise account of these matters elsewhere. Together with the dictator they appointed Marcus Minucius as master of the horse. This officer is placed under the commander-in-chief, but becomes, as it were, his deputy in the holder's absences on other business.

## Book 3 Chapter 88: Hannibal Marches Through Iapygia

Hannibal, shifting his camp from place to place over short distances, lingered in the region along the Adriatic. Because he had a great supply of old wine, he washed down his horses with it and so cured them of their poor condition and their mange.

In much the same way he restored his men, healing the wounded and bringing the rest into good physical shape and a keen readiness for the tasks ahead.

Then, after passing through and laying waste the territories of Praetutia and Hadria, and further those of the Marrucini and the Frentani, he set out and made his march into Iapygia.

This region is divided under three names—its peoples being called Daunii, Peucetii, and Messapii—and the first district he invaded was Daunia.

Beginning there from Luceria, which is a Roman colony, he plundered the countryside.

After this he encamped near the place called Vibo, overran the territory of Arpi, and ravaged all of Daunia without opposition.

At this same time Fabius, after his appointment, sacrificed to the gods and then set out together with his master of the horse and the four legions that had been enrolled for the occasion.

Joining the forces that had come to his aid from Ariminum near Narnia, he relieved Gnaeus, the existing commander, of the land command and sent him off under escort to Rome, with instructions that, should the Carthaginians make any movement by sea, he should always come to the rescue as circumstances required.

Fabius himself, with his master of the horse, took over the forces and encamped facing the Carthaginians near the place called Aecae, keeping about fifty stades from the enemy.

## Book 3 Chapter 89: Fabius Defers Battle

Hannibal, realizing that Fabius had arrived and wishing to strike fear into his opponents by an immediate assault, led out his army, drew close to the Roman entrenchment, and formed up for battle. But after waiting for some time, with no one coming out against him, he again withdrew to his own camp.

For Fabius had resolved neither to expose himself to risk nor to stake everything on a battle, but to make the safety of those under his command his first and foremost aim; and he held firmly to this decision.

At the outset he was despised for it and gave occasion for talk that he had turned coward and was terrified of the danger. But in time he compelled everyone to admit and agree that no one could possibly have handled the circumstances then prevailing with greater sense or prudence.

And events soon bore witness in favor of his reasoning—and reasonably so.

For it happened that the enemy's forces had been continuously trained in warfare from their earliest years; that they had as their leader a man brought up among them and schooled from boyhood in operations in the field;

that they had won many battles in Iberia, and had twice in succession beaten the Romans and their allies; and, most important of all, that having given up everything else, they had one single hope of survival—in victory.

With the Roman army the very opposite of all this was the case.

For this reason Fabius was unable to commit to a decisive engagement, since his inferiority was plain to see. Instead, falling back in his calculations upon his own advantages, he kept to these and conducted the war by their means.

And the Romans' advantages were inexhaustible resources

## Book 3 Chapter 90: Hannibal Enters Campania

and an abundance of manpower. And so, in the period that followed, he kept maneuvering alongside the enemy, and by his experience he would seize beforehand all the favorable positions.

Since he had ample supplies at his back, he never let his soldiers go out foraging or get separated from the camp at all, but kept them always concentrated and massed together, watching for the right places and moments.

And many of the enemy who, out of contempt for him, strayed from their own camp to forage he captured and destroyed in this manner.

He did this with a double purpose: at once to keep whittling down the enemy from their fixed numbers, and at the same time gradually to build up and restore the spirits of his own troops, which had been beaten down in the larger contests, through these successes in detail.

But to come down to a decisive trial of strength by mutual agreement he was in no way willing.

None of this, however, pleased Marcus, his master of the horse. Currying favor with the crowd, he disparaged Fabius to everyone, alleging that he was conducting affairs in an ignoble and sluggish way, while he himself was eager to take the risk and fight it out.

The Carthaginians, after laying waste the districts mentioned, crossed the Apennines and descended into the land of Samnium—a prosperous country untouched by war for many years—and found themselves amid such abundance of provisions that they could not exhaust the plunder by use or by destruction. They also overran the territory of Beneventum,

which is a Roman colony, and took the city of Venusia, which was unwalled and full of property of every kind in great quantity.

The Romans kept following continually behind, staying one or two days' march away, yet they were unable to come near or grapple with the enemy.

Therefore Hannibal, seeing that Fabius was plainly avoiding battle but was not on the whole giving up the open country, made a bold move into the plains around Capua, and within them to the place called Falernum,

convinced that one of two things would result: either he would force the enemy to fight, or he would make it clear to all that he was master of the field and that the Romans were yielding the open country to him.

Should that happen, he hoped the cities, struck with dismay, would be moved to revolt from Rome.

For up to that time, though the Romans had now been defeated in two battles, not a single city in Italy had gone over to the Carthaginians; they all kept their loyalty, even though some were suffering badly.

From this one may gauge the awe and esteem the Roman state inspired among its allies.

## Book 3 Chapter 91: Fertility and Beauty of the Plains Near Capua

And in fact Hannibal had good reason for arriving at these calculations.

For the plains around Capua are the most renowned in all Italy, both for their richness and their beauty and because they lie right on the sea and have at their disposal those trading ports into which sailors bound for Italy run from nearly every part of the inhabited world.

They also contain within them the most famous and most beautiful cities of Italy.

Their coastline is occupied by the people of Sinuessa, of Cumae, and of Puteoli, and besides these the Neapolitans, and lastly the nation of the Nucerians.

Of the interior, the parts toward the north are inhabited by the people of Cales and of Teanum, and those toward the east and south by the Daunii*

and the Nolans. In the very center of the plains lies Capua, the city that was once the most blessed of all.

The story told even by the mythographers about these plains is most plausible: these too are called the Phlegraean plains, just like others among the famous plains. And it is most likely that the gods quarreled over these in particular because of their beauty and their fertility.

Along with the advantages already mentioned, the plains are thought to be strong and altogether difficult to enter; for they are enclosed on one side by the sea and for the greater part by great mountains, continuous on every side, through which there are only three passes from the interior, narrow and hard to traverse:

one from Samnium, a second from Latium, and the last from the region around the Hirpini.

For this reason the Carthaginians, by encamping in these plains as in a theater, were bound to strike everyone with astonishment at the unexpected sight, to expose their enemies as cowards shrinking from battle, and to show themselves beyond dispute the masters of the open country.

## Book 3 Chapter 92: Hannibal Selects Winter Quarters

Reasoning along these lines, then, Hannibal marched out of Samnite territory through the pass by the hill called Eribianus and encamped beside the river Vulturnus, which divides the plains just described into roughly two halves.

He kept his camp on the side facing Rome, and with his foraging parties he ranged over the whole plain and plundered it without hindrance.

Fabius was thoroughly alarmed at the enemy's daring stroke, but for that very reason he held all the more firmly to the course he had decided upon.

His colleague Marcus, however, along with all the military tribunes and company commanders in the army, believed they had caught the enemy in an excellent position, and thought they ought to press on, close with them on the plain, and not stand by while the most celebrated part of the country was being ravaged.

Fabius pressed forward only as far as reaching the area, going along with those who were eager and ready to take risks,

but once he had drawn near to Falernum, he showed himself along the lower slopes and kept pace with the enemy, so as not to seem to his own allies to be surrendering the open country.

He would not, however, bring his army down into the plain, taking care to avoid an all-out engagement, both for the reasons already mentioned and because the enemy was plainly far superior in cavalry.

As for Hannibal, when he had tested the enemy and ravaged the entire plain, gathering an immense quantity of plunder,

he set about breaking camp, intending not to squander the booty but to deposit it in a place where he could also pass the winter, so that the army might have not merely a present feast but a steady abundance of supplies.

Fabius understood his plan—that he was preparing to make his return by the same route by which he had entered—and seeing that the ground was narrow and exceptionally well suited for an attack,

he stationed about four thousand men at the defile itself, urging them to use their courage at the right moment together with the natural advantage of the terrain, while he himself, with the greater part of his force, took up a position on a commanding hill in front of the narrows.

## Book 3 Chapter 93: The Cattle With the Burning Fagots

...he encamped. When the Carthaginians arrived and pitched their camp on the level ground right at the foot of the slope, he expected to carry off their plunder without a fight, and even, in all likelihood, to put an end to the whole affair, thanks to the favorable lie of the land.

So he was occupied with these deliberations and bent upon them, considering where and how he should make use of the terrain, and which men were to begin the attack on the enemy, and from what quarter.

But Hannibal, while the enemy was making these preparations for the coming day, reasoned out the likely course of events and gave them no time or opportunity to carry out their designs.

He summoned Hasdrubal, the officer in charge of the work details, and ordered him to bundle together torches from dry brushwood of every kind, as many as possible and with all speed, and to pick out from the whole of the plunder the sturdiest of the draft oxen, about two thousand of them, and collect them in front of the camp.

When this was done, he gathered the work crews together and pointed out to them a certain ridge lying between his own camp and the narrows through which he intended to march; toward this ridge he ordered them to drive the oxen hard and by force, once the order was given, until they reached the heights.

After this he told them all to take their supper and rest at the proper hour.

As soon as the third part of the night had passed, he at once led out the work crews and ordered them to fasten the torches to the oxen's horns.

This was quickly done because of their numbers, and he gave the order to light them all and directed the men to drive the oxen forward and force them up toward the ridge tops,

while he posted the spearmen behind them, telling them to help the drivers up to a certain point, but, once the animals had taken their first headlong rush, to run out along the flanks and, raising a din, to make for the high ground and seize the ridge tops in advance, so that they might lend support and engage the enemy if they should meet any at the heights.

At this same moment he himself moved out, taking first the heavy infantry, behind them the cavalry, next the booty, and after all the rest the Iberians and Celts...

## Book 3 Chapter 94: Fabius Returns to Rome

...he came to the narrows and the defiles. As for the Romans guarding the narrows, the moment they saw the lights advancing toward the heights, they supposed Hannibal was making his push that way, and so they abandoned the difficult ground and hurried to the help of the heights.

But as they drew near the oxen they were thrown into confusion by the lights, imagining and expecting something greater and more terrible than what was actually happening. Then, when the Carthaginian spearmen arrived,

after the two sides had exchanged a few long-range shots, with the oxen now charging in among them, both parties drew apart and held to the heights, waiting expectantly for the coming of day, since they could not make out what was going on.

Fabius, for his part, was partly baffled at what was taking place and, in the poet's words, "suspected it was some trick," and partly, in keeping with his original resolve, by no means judged it right to throw the dice or stake everything on a general engagement; so he kept quiet within his palisade and waited for daylight.

Meanwhile Hannibal, his plan succeeding as he had intended, brought his force safely through the narrows along with the booty, since those guarding the difficult ground had abandoned their posts.

At daybreak, observing the men stationed on the heights facing his spearmen, he sent over some of the Iberians, who closed with the Romans, cut down about a thousand of them, and easily relieved their own light troops and brought them down.

So Hannibal, having made his exit from Falernum in this fashion, now camped in safety and proceeded to survey and plan where and how he should pass the winter, having instilled great fear and much bewilderment in the cities and peoples of Italy.

Fabius, meanwhile, was spoken of badly by the masses, on the grounds that he had unmanfully let the enemy slip away from such ground; yet he did not abandon his purpose.

And being compelled, a few days later, to go to Rome for certain sacrifices, he handed the legions over to his colleague, and as he departed he charged him repeatedly not to be as eager to harm the enemy as to see that his own men suffered no serious hurt.

But Marcus took not the slightest of this to heart, and even while Fabius was still speaking he was wholly and utterly bent on hazarding battle and risking all.

## Book 3 Chapter 95: Hasdrubal Equips a Fleet

Such, then, was the situation in Italy.

Around the same time as the events just described, Hasdrubal, the general appointed over Iberia, had during the winter refitted the thirty ships left him by his brother and manned ten more; and at the beginning of summer he put to sea from New Carthage with forty decked vessels, having appointed Hamilcar admiral of the fleet.

At the same time he assembled his land force out of its winter quarters and set off: with the ships he made his voyage close along the shore, and with the infantry his march along the beach, hastening to bring both forces together at the river Ebro.

Gnaeus, reckoning up the designs of the Carthaginians, at first intended to come out of his winter quarters and meet them both by land and by sea.

But on hearing of the size of their forces and the scale of their preparations, he gave up the idea of meeting them by land; instead he manned thirty-five ships and, taking from his land army the men best suited for service as marines, he put to sea and on the second day made the run from Tarraco to the region of the river Ebro.

Coming to anchor about eighty stades from the enemy, he sent ahead two fast-sailing Massiliot ships to reconnoiter; for these men took the lead and the first risks, and rendered every service to the Romans without stint.

For the people of Massilia, if any others ever did, nobly shared in the fortunes of Rome—often on later occasions, but most of all during the war with Hannibal.

When the men sent out to reconnoiter reported that the enemy's fleet happened to be lying at anchor off the mouth of the river, Scipio put to sea in haste, wishing to fall upon them suddenly...

## Book 3 Chapter 96: Naval Success of the Romans In Spain

Hasdrubal and his men, having been warned well in advance by their scouts that the enemy was bearing down on them, drew up their land forces along the shore and at the same time ordered the crews to embark in the ships.

When the Romans were already close at hand, they gave the signal for battle and put out to sea, having resolved to fight. They engaged the enemy and for a short while contended for the victory, but before long they began to give way.

For the support of the infantry stationed along the shore did them less good in lending them courage for the danger than it did harm by holding out a ready hope of safety.

In the end, after losing two ships together with their crews, and the oar-banks and marines of four others, they fled, turning aside toward the land.

As the Romans pressed on against them with fury, they ran their ships up onto the beach and, leaping out of the vessels, made their escape to the troops drawn up there.

The Romans came boldly right up to the shore, took in tow such of the vessels as could still be moved, and sailed off in overwhelming joy, having beaten the enemy at the first onset, gained command of the sea, and captured twenty-five of their ships.

So in Iberia, as a result of this, the prospects of the Romans had grown more promising on account of the success just described.

The Carthaginians, when news of this setback reached them, at once manned seventy ships and sent them out, having judged it essential, for the sake of all their designs, to keep their hold on the sea.

These ships made first for Sardinia, and from there put in at the region around Pisa in Italy, since those aboard were convinced that they would link up there with Hannibal's forces.

But the Romans quickly put out against them from Rome itself with a hundred and twenty quinqueremes, and when the Carthaginians learned of this advance, they sailed back again to Sardinia and after that returned once more to Carthage.

Gnaeus Servilius, who commanded the fleet just mentioned, followed the Carthaginians for some distance, convinced that he would overtake them, but as he fell far behind he gave up the chase.

He first put in at Lilybaeum in Sicily; after that he sailed down to Libya, to the island of the Cercinitae, and after taking money from them on condition of not ravaging their territory, he departed.

On the voyage back he gained control of the island of Cossyrus and, after installing a garrison in its little town, he put in again at Lilybaeum.

For the rest, having moored his fleet there, after no long time he himself

## Book 3 Chapter 97: Spanish Hostages Given Up To the Scipios

went back to the land forces. Meanwhile the Senate, learning of the advantage that Gnaeus had won in the sea battle, and considering it useful—or rather essential—not to abandon affairs in Iberia, but to make a stand against the Carthaginians and to press the war forward,

made ready twenty ships and put Publius Scipio in command of them, in accordance with the plan formed at the outset, and dispatched him in haste to his brother Gnaeus, to manage the campaign in Iberia jointly with him.

For they were deeply anxious that the Carthaginians might gain control of those regions and, securing abundant supplies and manpower, lay claim to the sea more completely and join in the attack on Italy, sending armies and money to Hannibal.

For this reason, regarding this war too as of great importance, they sent out the ships and Publius. On reaching Iberia and joining his brother, he rendered great service to the common cause.

For never before had the Romans ventured to cross the river Iber—they had been content with the friendship and alliance of the tribes on the near side—but now they crossed it, and for the first time found the courage to lay claim to affairs on the far side, with chance, too, lending them considerable help in the circumstances that surrounded them.

For after overawing the Iberians living about the crossing, they came to the city of the Saguntines and pitched camp about forty stades away, near the temple of Aphrodite,

having taken up a position naturally well suited both for safety from the enemy and for the supply of provisions from the sea;

for it happened that their fleet was at the same time making its passage along the coast beside them. It was there that

## Book 3 Chapter 98: Treason of Abilyx

a reversal of affairs of the following kind took place. At the time when Hannibal was making his march to Italy, from all the cities of Iberia whose loyalty he distrusted he took as hostages the sons of the most prominent men, and he deposited them all in the city of the Saguntines, both because of its strength and because of the loyalty of the men left in charge of it. Now there was a certain Iberian,

Abilyx by name, second to none of the Iberians in standing and in the circumstances of his life, and reputed to surpass all the rest by far in his goodwill and loyalty toward the Carthaginians.

This man, observing how affairs stood and judging that the prospects of the Romans were the more promising, worked out in his own mind a calculation about betraying the hostages—a calculation thoroughly Iberian and barbarian.

For, convinced that he could rise to great power among the Romans if he offered, at the critical moment, a proof of loyalty together with a useful service, he set about breaking faith with the Carthaginians and handing the hostages over to the Romans.

He observed that Bostar, the Carthaginian general—who had been sent by Hasdrubal to stop the Romans from crossing the river, but, not daring to do this, had withdrawn and was encamped in the parts of Saguntum facing the sea—was a guileless man, gentle by nature,

and well-disposed and trusting toward himself; so he opened the matter of the hostages to Bostar, saying that, now that the Romans had crossed the river, the Carthaginians could no longer hold Iberia together by fear, but that the situation called for the goodwill of their subjects;

now therefore, with the Romans drawn near and laying siege to Saguntum, and the city in danger, if Bostar were to bring out the hostages and restore them to their parents and their cities, he would frustrate the ambition of the Romans—for this was the very thing they were most eager to accomplish, by getting control of the hostages—

and he would call forth the goodwill of all the Iberians toward the Carthaginians, since he had foreseen what was coming and had taken thought for the safety of the hostages. And he said that he would multiply the favor many times over by personally taking charge of the affair.

For, by restoring the boys to their cities, he would win over the goodwill not only of those who had fathered them but also of the people at large, setting before their eyes, through what was happening, the chosen policy and magnanimity of the Carthaginians toward their allies.

He urged Bostar also to expect a host of gifts privately from those who recovered their children; for each of them, unexpectedly regaining the dearest of their kin, would compete in showering benefits on the man in charge of the affair.

By arguing these points and many others like them in the same vein, he persuaded Bostar to agree to

## Book 3 Chapter 99: The Boys are Restored to Their Native Cities

what he proposed. And for the time being Abilyx went away, having fixed a day on which he would come with everything needed for conveying the boys back.

Arriving by night at the Roman camp and falling in with some of the Iberians serving with the Romans, through them he came before the generals.

Reckoning up at length the surge of feeling and the change of allegiance toward them that would come about among the Iberians if they gained control of the hostages, he undertook to hand the boys over to them.

Publius and his colleague received the prospect with the greatest eagerness and promised large rewards, and for the moment Abilyx went off to his own country, having agreed on the day, the hour, and the place at which those who were to receive him would have to wait.

After this he took the friends he needed and came to Bostar, and when the boys had been handed over to him from Saguntum, he set out by night, as though wishing to escape notice, slipped past the enemy's stockade, and came at the appointed time and place and delivered all the hostages into the hands of the Roman commanders.

Publius and his colleague honored Abilyx exceptionally and made use of him for the restoration of the hostages to their homelands, sending along their own trusted men.

Going from city to city and, through the restoration of the boys, setting before everyone's eyes the mildness and magnanimity of the Romans in contrast to the faithlessness and harshness of the Carthaginians, and adding to this the example of his own change of sides, he spurred many of the Iberians on toward friendship with the Romans.

Bostar, having shown himself, in handing the hostages over to the enemy, more childish than befitted his years, fell into no ordinary dangers.

For the present, with the season now pressing, both sides broke up their forces into winter quarters, the affair of the boys having proved a considerable piece of luck for the Romans in view of the designs that lay before them. Such was the state of affairs in Iberia.

## Book 3 Chapter 100: Hannibal In Apulia

The general Hannibal—to pick up where we left off—learned from his scouts that there was a very large supply of grain in the territory around Luceria and the place called Geronium, and that Geronium was well suited for collecting it.

He therefore decided to make his winter quarters there, and advanced, marching past Mount Liburnum toward the places just mentioned. When he reached Geronium,

which lies two hundred stades from Luceria, he at first tried through negotiation to win the inhabitants over to friendship and offered them guarantees of his promises; but when no one would listen, he set about besieging it.

He quickly took control of the town, put the inhabitants to death, but kept most of the houses and the walls intact, intending to use them as grain stores for the winter.

He stationed his army in front of the city and fortified the camp with a trench and palisade.

Once this was done, he sent two-thirds of his force out to gather grain, ordering each man to bring back a fixed measure every day for his own unit, this being the assigned quota for those put in charge of this management,

while with the remaining third he guarded the camp and watched over the foragers at various points.

Since most of the countryside was easily traversed and flat, the men gathering the grain were practically beyond counting, and the season was at its peak for the harvest, an immense quantity of grain came to be collected every day.

## Book 3 Chapter 101: Successes of Minucius

Marcus, having taken over the forces from Fabius, at first kept pace with the enemy along the mountain ridges, convinced that sooner or later he would clash with the Carthaginians somewhere at the passes.

But when he heard that Hannibal's men already held Geronium, were foraging the countryside for grain, and were encamped behind a palisade thrown up in front of the city, he turned away from the ridges and came down by the spur that runs out toward the plains.

Arriving at the height that lies in the territory of Larinum and is called Calene, he encamped near it, ready by any means whatever to engage the enemy.

When Hannibal saw the enemy approaching, he left a third of his force to forage, and taking the other two-thirds advanced sixteen stades from the city and encamped on a hill facing the enemy, intending both to intimidate his opponents and to provide security for his foragers.

After this, since there was a low hill between the two camps, conveniently situated and lying close to the enemy's position, he sent out about two thousand of his spearmen while it was still night and seized it.

When day came and Marcus caught sight of them, he led out his light-armed troops and assaulted the hill.

After a spirited skirmish, the Romans finally prevailed, and afterward they moved their whole camp to this spot.

For a while, because the camps faced each other, Hannibal kept the greater part of his force close to himself.

But as more days passed, he was forced to detach some men to pasture the livestock and others to forage for grain,

being eager—in keeping with his original plan—both to avoid spoiling his plunder and to gather as much grain as possible, so that there would be an abundance of everything for his men during the winter, and no less for the pack animals and the horses;

for he placed the greatest hopes of his army in his cavalry corps.

## Book 3 Chapter 102: The Romans Capture the Carthaginian Foragers

It was at this point that Marcus, observing that a large part of the enemy was scattered about the countryside on the tasks just described, picked the most favorable hour of the day and led out his army.

Coming up close to the Carthaginian camp, he drew up his heavy infantry in line, and dividing his cavalry and light troops into detachments, sent them against the foragers with orders to take no prisoners.

When this happened, Hannibal fell into great difficulty: he was strong enough neither to march out against the troops drawn up before him nor to relieve his men scattered about the countryside.

Of the Romans, those sent against the foragers killed many of the scattered men, while the troops drawn up in line finally reached such a pitch of contempt that they even began tearing down the palisade and all but besieging the Carthaginians.

Hannibal was in dire straits, yet even under this storm he held on, beating off those who came near and barely keeping his camp,

until Hasdrubal, gathering up the men who had fled from the countryside into the camp near Geronium—about four thousand of them—came to his aid.

Then, taking a little courage, he sallied out, drew up his line a short distance in front of the camp, and with difficulty fended off the immediate danger.

Marcus, having killed many of the enemy in the fighting around the palisade and still more out in the countryside, withdrew for the time being, with high hopes for what was to come.

The next day, when the Carthaginians abandoned the palisade, he advanced and occupied their camp.
