Since, however, the young men who had come in were many, and someone made clear to him the force surrounding the house outside, he gave way to the circumstances and went along with his friends.

## Book 18 Chapter 54: Scopas and Dicaearchus Punished

As soon as Scopas entered the council chamber, the king first stated the charge against him briefly; after the king came Polycrates, who had just arrived from Cyprus, and last of all Aristomenes.

In all other respects the accusation made by them all was much the same as what has just been described, but to the previous charges there was now added the council he had held with his friends and his refusal to obey when summoned by the king.

On these grounds not only did all the members of the council condemn him, but so did the foreign envoys who were present.

When Aristomenes was about to make his accusation, he brought in many other distinguished men from Greece, as well as the ambassadors sent by the Aetolians to negotiate a settlement, among whom was Dorimachus son of Nicostratus.

When these speeches had been delivered, Scopas in turn tried to offer some pleas in his defense; but since no one paid him any attention, because of the senselessness of his conduct, he was immediately led off to prison along with his friends.

Then, when night came, Aristomenes had Scopas and all his relatives and friends put to death by poison;

but Dicaearchus he subjected to the rack and the scourge, and so made an end of him, exacting from him a penalty that was fitting and shared on behalf of all the Greeks.

For this was the Dicaearchus whom Philip, when he set out to violate his treaties against the Cyclades and the cities on the Hellespont, appointed commander of the whole fleet and director of the entire operation.

Sent out to commit such open impiety, he not only thought he was doing nothing strange, but in the extravagance of his madness supposed that he would strike terror even into the gods as well as into men.

For wherever he anchored his ships he set up two altars, one to Impiety and one to Lawlessness, and on these he sacrificed and to these he bowed down as though they were divine powers.

For this reason it seems to me that he met with the punishment he deserved from both gods and men: having set the course of his own life against nature, fittingly he met an end against nature too at the hands of destiny.

As for the rest of the Aetolians, the king let all those who wished to return to their own country depart with their possessions.

## Book 18 Chapter 55: Anacleteria of Ptolemy Epiphanes

Scopas's love of money had been conspicuous even while he was alive—for in his greed he far surpassed all other men—but after his death it became even more apparent through the quantity of gold and the goods that were found in his possession.

For taking as his accomplice the savagery and the drunkenness of Charimortus, he had utterly plundered the kingdom to its very foundations.

Now once the courtiers had settled the affair of the Aetolians satisfactorily, they at once set about performing the Anacleteria of the king. His age did not yet make this pressing, but they thought that affairs would gain a certain stability and a fresh start toward better progress if the king were regarded as having now come into full power.

So, making their preparations on a magnificent scale, they carried out the proceedings in a manner worthy of the dignity of the kingdom, with Polycrates thought to have contributed the most toward this undertaking.

For the man just mentioned, even in the reign of the king's father, while he was still young, was reckoned second to none at court either in trustworthiness or in achievement, and likewise so under the present king.

For having been entrusted with Cyprus and its revenues at times that were dangerous and unsettled, he not only preserved the island for the boy-king, but also amassed a considerable sum of money, which he had now come bringing to the king, after handing over the governorship of Cyprus to Ptolemy of Megalopolis.

Having for these reasons won great approval and wealth in the years that followed, he afterward, as he advanced in age, drifted completely into licentiousness and a debauched life.

A reputation rather similar to his was inherited in old age by Ptolemy son of Agesarchus as well.

Concerning these men, when we come to the proper occasions, we shall not hesitate to set out plainly the disgraceful things that attended their exercise of power.

# Polybius — The Histories, Book XIX

Modern English translation of the Greek text.

## Book 19 Chapter 1: Summary Based on Livy

I. Affairs of Italy

Polybius says that he ordered the walls of all the cities on this side of the Baetis to be pulled down in a single day; there were a great many such cities, and they were full of fighting men.

## Book 19 Chapter 2

II. Affairs of Greece

There was a vast number of prisoners taken in the Punic War. When their own people did not ransom them, Hannibal sold them. The scale of the matter is shown by what Polybius writes: it cost the Achaeans one hundred talents, since they fixed the payment to be returned to the owners at five hundred denarii for each man.

# Polybius — The Histories, Book XX

Modern English translation of the Greek text.

## Book 20 Chapter 1: Greece: Antiochus and the Aetolians Meet

Olympiad 147, year 1. Greek Affairs.

And again from Polybius: they appointed thirty of the Apocleti to sit in council together with the king. And again: he convened the Apocleti and laid before them a deliberation concerning the present situation.

## Book 20 Chapter 2: The Boeotians Answer Antiochus

When Philip sent an embassy to the Boeotians, the Boeotians replied to the envoys that, once the king came to them in person, they would then deliberate about the proposals being urged upon them.

## Book 20 Chapter 3: Epirus and Elis Ask Antiochus for Help

While Antiochus was staying at Chalcis and winter was beginning, envoys came to him: from the Epirote nation, the embassy headed by Charops, and from the city of the Eleans, the embassy headed by Callistratus.

The Epirotes urged him not to drag them prematurely into the war against the Romans, since he could see that they lay directly in the path facing Italy ahead of all the rest of Greece.

If, however, he could himself take up a forward position to defend Epirus and secure their safety, they said they would receive him into both their cities and their harbors;

but if he judged it best not to do this for the present, they asked him to pardon them for being afraid of a war with the Romans.

The Eleans, for their part, urged him to send help to their city, since, now that the Achaeans had voted for war, they were wary of an attack from them.

The king answered the Epirotes that he would send envoys to discuss with them what was in their common interest,

while to the Eleans he dispatched a thousand foot soldiers, putting Euphanes the Cretan in command.

## Book 20 Chapter 4: The Decline of Boeotia

The Boeotians had for a long time now been in a poor condition, one that stood in stark contrast to the former vigor and renown of their state.

For these people, having won great glory and great power in the days of the battle of Leuctra, somehow—I cannot say how—steadily kept losing both of the qualities just mentioned in the years that followed, under the leadership of Abaeocritus.

And from that time on they not only kept losing them, but, turning altogether to the opposite course, they obscured their earlier reputation as far as they were able.

For when the Achaeans had stirred them up to war against the Aetolians, they adopted the same policy as the Achaeans and formed an alliance with them, and thereafter waged continual war against the Aetolians.

But when the Aetolians invaded Boeotia with an army, the Boeotians marched out in full force, and—although the Achaeans had assembled and were about to come to their aid—they did not wait for their arrival but engaged the Aetolians.

Being defeated in the battle, they were so crushed in spirit that, from that campaign on, they no longer dared to lay claim to any honorable distinction at all, nor did they share with the other Greeks in any common undertaking or contest decided by joint resolution.

Instead, having given themselves over to feasting and drunkenness, they grew slack not only in their bodies but in their souls as well.

## Book 20 Chapter 5: Continued Decline of Boeotia

The main stages of the Boeotians' gradual decline into folly came about among them in the following way.

Immediately after the defeat mentioned above, they abandoned the Achaeans and attached their nation to the Aetolians.

But when, some time later, the Aetolians in turn went to war with Demetrius, the father of Philip, the Boeotians abandoned them as well; and when Demetrius came into Boeotia with an army, they made no trial of the dangers of resistance but submitted themselves wholly to the Macedonians.

Yet, since a faint flicker of their ancestral glory still lingered, there were some who were displeased with the present state of affairs and with the policy of obeying the Macedonians in everything.

For this reason there came to be strong political opposition between these men and the party of Ascondas and Neon, the ancestors of Brachylles; for these were the men who at that time leaned most strongly toward Macedonia.

In the end, however, the party of Ascondas gained the upper hand, owing to a turn of events of the following kind.

After the death of Demetrius, Antigonus, who was acting as Philip's guardian, was sailing on some business toward the outermost parts of Boeotia, in the direction of Larymna, when an unexpected ebb of the tide left his ships stranded on dry land.

Just at this moment a report had reached the Boeotians that Antigonus intended to overrun their territory. Neon, who was then commander of the cavalry and was leading all the Boeotian horse about with him to guard the country, came upon Antigonus and his men while they were at a loss and helpless because of what had happened.

And though he had it in his power to inflict serious harm on the Macedonians, he decided, contrary to their expectation, to spare them.

This action of his pleased the rest of the Boeotians, but it did not please the Thebans at all.

Antigonus, however, when the tide flowed back a little later and his ships were lifted free, felt deep gratitude toward Neon for not having joined in attacking them during their misfortune; and he himself completed the voyage to Asia on which he had set out.

And so afterward, when he had defeated the Spartan Cleomenes and become master of Lacedaemon, he left Brachylles as governor of the city, repaying him in this way for the good service done by his father Neon. From these favors the house of Brachylles came to be restored to no small degree.

Nor was this the only consideration Antigonus showed them; rather, continuously—now he himself, now Philip—supplying them with funds and constantly lending them strength, they quickly overcame the rival political party in Thebes and forced everyone, except a very few, to side with Macedonia.

Such, then, was the beginning that the affairs of the house of Neon took, and of its alliance with the Macedonians—

## Book 20 Chapter 6: Disorganised State of Boeotia

—and of the increase of its fortune. Meanwhile the public affairs of the Boeotians had fallen into such a wretched condition that for nearly twenty-five years justice had not been administered among them, neither in private contracts nor in public charges.

Instead, some of the magistrates would order the dispatch of garrisons and others would proclaim national levies, and in this way they continually obstructed the course of justice; and some of the generals even made payments out of the public funds to the poor among the people.

From this the masses were taught to attach themselves to such men and to secure offices for them—men through whom they could expect to pay no penalty for their crimes and debts, and from time to time to gain some share of public property through the favor of those in office. The man who contributed most to this state of things was

Opheltas, who was forever devising some new scheme that seemed for the moment to benefit the many, but was bound in the end, by general admission, to ruin them all.

Along with these things followed another unfortunate fashion. Those who died childless no longer left their property to their relatives, as had earlier been the custom among them, but assigned it to feasting and drinking and made it common property for their friends.

And many even of those who had children would distribute the greater part of their estate to their dining clubs, so that there were many Boeotians who had more dinners in the month than there were days allotted to the month.

For this reason the Megarians, hating such a state of affairs and remembering their former membership in the federation alongside the Achaeans, once more turned away toward the Achaeans and their party.

For the Megarians had originally been part of the Achaean political community from the time of Antigonus Gonatas; but when Cleomenes took up a position on the Isthmus, being cut off they attached themselves to the Boeotians with the consent of the Achaeans.

A little before the times now under discussion, becoming dissatisfied with the Boeotian government, they once again turned back toward the Achaeans.

The Boeotians, enraged at what they regarded as contempt, marched out against the Megarians in full force under arms.

And when the Megarians took no notice at all of their arrival, the Boeotians, thus provoked, set about besieging the city and launching assaults on it.

But when a panic fell upon them, together with a rumor that Philopoemen had arrived with the Achaeans, they left their scaling-ladders against the wall and fled headlong back to their own land.

## Book 20 Chapter 7: Fortune and Degeneracy of the Boeotians

With their politics in such a condition, the Boeotians somehow slipped through, by good luck, even the crises of the times of Philip and of Antiochus.

In the period that followed, however, they did not escape; rather, as if Fortune were deliberately exacting requital, she seemed to come down heavily upon them—matters of which we shall make mention in what follows. —

The majority put forward, as the pretext for their estrangement from the Romans, the killing of Brachylles and the campaign that Titus made against Coronea on account of the murders of Romans that were taking place on the roads;

but in truth they were diseased in their souls because of the causes already described.

For when the king drew near, the leading men of the Boeotians went out to meet him; and after joining him and conversing in a friendly manner, they conducted him into Thebes. —

## Book 20 Chapter 8: Submission of the Aetolian Officers

Antiochus, the one called the Great, whom the Romans brought down—as Polybius records in his twentieth book—came to Chalcis in Euboea and celebrated his marriage there. He was fifty years old and had taken upon himself the two greatest of undertakings: the liberation of the Greeks, as he himself proclaimed it, and the war against the Romans.

Having fallen in love with a young Chalcidian girl in the very midst of the war, he set his heart on marrying her, being a heavy drinker and one who delighted in drunken revels.

She was the daughter of Cleoptolemus, one of the men of distinction, and she surpassed all other women in beauty.

And while celebrating his marriage there in Chalcis, he spent the whole winter on the spot, taking not the slightest thought for the business at hand; and he gave the girl the name Euboea.

So when he was defeated in the war, he fled to Ephesus with his new bride.

And out of his whole army, except for the five hundred or so who were around the king, scarcely anyone escaped; and even of the ten thousand soldiers whom—on Polybius' authority—we have recorded that the king brought across with him into Greece, only a tiny number survived.

## Book 20 Chapter 9: The Aetolians Seek a Truce

After Heracleia had fallen into Roman hands, Phaeneas, the general of the Aetolians, and those around him saw the crisis now closing in on Aetolia, and, keeping before their eyes what was bound to happen to the other cities, they resolved to send envoys to Manius to ask for a truce and a settlement.

Having decided on this, they sent out Archedamus, Pantaleon, and Chalepus.

When these men met with the Roman general, they intended to make a rather long speech, but they were cut off in the middle of the interview and prevented from continuing.

For Manius said that at the present moment he had no time to spare, being preoccupied with managing the spoils taken from Heracleia.

He told them, however, that he would grant a ten-day truce and would send Lucius along with them, and he instructed them to lay before Lucius whatever requests they had.

Once the truce had been made and Lucius had come to Hypata, a considerable discussion took place about the present situation.

The Aetolians built up their case by going back over the past, citing the acts of goodwill they had earlier shown toward the Romans.

But Lucius cut their enthusiasm short, saying that this kind of pleading did not fit the present circumstances; for since their original friendly relations had been dissolved by the Aetolians themselves, and the present hostility had come about because of the Aetolians, the goodwill of those earlier times contributed nothing to the present situation.

He therefore advised them to give up arguing the rights of their case and to turn instead to the language of entreaty, begging the general to grant them pardon for their offenses.

After discussing their predicament at still greater length, the Aetolians decided to entrust the whole matter to Manius, committing themselves to the good faith of the Romans—

not knowing what force this carried, but misled by the word "faith," as though through it a more complete mercy would be extended to them.

But among the Romans, to put oneself into another's "faith" carries exactly the same force as to hand over to the victor full discretion over oneself.

## Book 20 Chapter 10: The Aetolians Do Not Confirm the Terms

Having decided on this, they sent Phaeneas and his colleagues off in haste together with Lucius to make the resolution clear to Manius.

When these men met with the general and once again pleaded their case in the same way on their own behalf, they concluded by declaring that the Aetolians had decided to commit themselves to the good faith of the Romans.

Manius took up their words and said: "So this is how matters stand,

men of Aetolia?" When they nodded assent, he went on: "Then, first of all, none of you must cross over into Asia, neither on your own account nor by any public decree;

second, you must hand over Dicaearchus and Menestratus the Epirote"—who happened at that time to have come to the aid of Naupactus—"and along with them King Amynander and those of the Athamanians who withdrew to your side together with him."

At this Phaeneas broke in and said: "But what you demand, general, is neither just nor in keeping with Greek ways."

Manius, not so much out of anger as from a wish to bring them to a sense of their situation and to thoroughly alarm them, replied: "Do you still play the Greek with me and talk about what is fitting and proper, after you have put yourselves into our good faith? I could bind every one of you in chains and march you off, if I saw fit."

As he said this, he ordered a chain to be brought and an iron collar to be fastened around each man's neck.

Phaeneas and his companions were struck dumb with shock and stood there speechless, as if paralyzed in body and soul at the unexpected turn of events.

But Lucius and some of the other military tribunes present begged Manius to take no harsh measures against the men before him, since they were in fact envoys. When he agreed, Phaeneas began to speak:

he said that he and the Apocleti would carry out the orders, but that the assent of the people too was needed if the demands were to be ratified.

Manius said he was right, and Phaeneas then asked that another ten-day truce be granted to them. When this too was conceded, they parted on these terms for the time being.

On reaching Hypata, they reported to the Apocleti what had happened and the words that had been spoken. On hearing this, the Aetolians then for the first time grasped how mistaken they had been and what compulsion was now bearing down on them.

It was therefore decided to write to the cities and call the Aetolians together to deliberate about the orders imposed on them.

But when the report of what had befallen Phaeneas and his party was spread abroad, the people became so enraged that no one was even willing to attend the meeting for deliberation.

Since this impossibility prevented any deliberation about the demands, and since at this very moment Nicander had sailed back from Asia into Phalara on the Malian gulf—the very place from which he had set out—and was reporting the king's eagerness toward him and his promises for the future, they grew even more dismissive, so that no conclusion at all was reached about peace.

And so, as soon as the days of the truce had passed, the war was once again firmly upon the Aetolians.

## Book 20 Chapter 11: The Fate of Nicander

The reversal of fortune that befell Nicander is not something to be passed over in silence.

He arrived back at Phalara from Ephesus on the twelfth day after the day he had set out.

He found the Romans still occupied around Heracleia, and the Macedonians, having withdrawn from Lamia, encamped not far from the city.

He got his money safely through into Lamia, against all expectation, and then attempted that night to slip across the ground between the two camps and into Hypata.

But he fell among the Macedonian pickets and was brought up to Philip while the king's banquet was still in full swing, expecting that he would suffer something terrible, falling under Philip's anger, or else be handed over to the Romans.

When the matter was reported to the king, however, Philip quickly ordered the officers in charge to look after Nicander and to treat him with every kindness.

After a while the king himself rose from the table and met with Nicander, and after roundly reproaching the general folly of the Aetolians—first for having brought the Romans against the Greeks, and after that Antiochus as well—he nevertheless urged them even now to forget the past, to hold fast to their goodwill toward him, and not to wish to press their advantage against one another in each other's hours of crisis.

He instructed Nicander to report this to the leaders of the Aetolians; and after urging Nicander himself to remember the kindness that had been shown him, he sent him off with a sufficient escort, ordering those assigned to the task to bring him safely back to Hypata.

Nicander, to whom this reception had appeared utterly unhoped-for and astonishing, was at that time brought back safely to his own people, and in the time that followed he remained, from this connection onward, well disposed to the house of Macedon.

And so, later, in the time of the war with Perseus, bound by the gratitude just described and finding it hard to work against the designs of Perseus, he fell under suspicion and slander, and was at last summoned to Rome, where he ended his life.

Corax: a mountain between Callipolis and Naupactus. Polybius, Book 20.

Aperanteia: a city of Thessaly. Polybius, Book 20.

## Book 20 Chapter 12: Philopoemen's Disinterestedness

...one of their own number to speak to him about these matters; but whereas, in the case of most men who undertake public work for profit, there are many ready to offer such favors and to make this the beginning of friendship and alliance, in the case of Philopoemen no one at all could be found willing to convey this favor to him,

until at last, being wholly at a loss, they chose by vote Timolaus. He, being both a hereditary guest-friend and long on familiar terms with Philopoemen, traveled twice to Megalopolis for this very purpose, yet did not dare to utter a word about the matter—until, spurring himself on and coming a third time, he found the courage to mention the gift.

Philopoemen, against all expectation, received him on this point graciously and kindly, and Timolaus was overjoyed,

supposing that he had achieved his aim. But Philopoemen said that he would come to Sparta himself within a few days, since he wished to thank all the magistrates for this honor.

He came afterward, and being invited into the council, he said that he had long known the goodwill of the Lacedaemonians toward him, but knew it best of all from the crown now being offered to him and from such an honor.

He said, then, that he accepted their intention, but was uneasy at the manner of it. For such honors and crowns, he said, ought not to be given to one's friends—since the man who puts on such a crown can never wash off its poison—but much rather to one's enemies,

so that friends, keeping their freedom of speech, may be trusted among the Achaeans whenever they propose to come to the city's aid, while enemies, having swallowed the bait, may be forced either to plead the Spartans' cause or, by keeping silent, be unable to do them any harm.

## II. Fragment of Uncertain Place

To form a judgment about events from hearsay is not the same as having been an eyewitness; the two differ greatly, and the conviction that comes from seeing a thing vividly for oneself naturally contributes much in every case.
